unit.can_do_en: say what I do and what I can do.

brief.situation_en: Leena needs help with her bike.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Osaatsä korjata pyörän? Mun rengas on puhki.
lines.text_kirja: Osaatko sinä korjata pyörän? Minun renkaani on puhki.
lines.gloss_en: Can you fix a bike? My tyre is flat.

judge.reason: Same question about repairing a bike and the tire being flat; only register differs.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: I can! My dad taught me.

judge.reason: Same: I can, my father taught me.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.gloss_en: Fantastic! I can't do it at all.

judge.reason: Same: great, I can't do it at all.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Do you have a repair kit?

judge.reason: Same question about having a repair kit.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Hyvä. Tää vie vaan kymmenen minuuttii.
lines.text_kirja: Hyvä. Tämä vie vain kymmenen minuuttia.
lines.gloss_en: Good. This only takes ten minutes.

judge.reason: Same: this only takes ten minutes.

lines.speaker: Leena
lines.text_puhe: Mä voin opettaa sulle neulomista vastineeks!
lines.text_kirja: Minä voin opettaa sinulle neulomista vastineeksi!
lines.gloss_en: I can teach you knitting in return!

judge.reason: Same offer to teach knitting in return.
Diili (slang 'deal') and Sovittu ('agreed') both mean deal; register difference only.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: osata means to know how. -t goes with sinä. Speech says osaatsä instead of -ko.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
A whole thing fixed takes -n: pyörä becomes pyörän.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books write renkaani, with -ni for 'my'. Speech says mun rengas and drops the ending.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': isäni. Speech says mun isä and drops the ending.
opettaa means to teach. In the past, for 'he' or 'she', it becomes opetti.
Minä with -lle for 'for'. Speech shortens it to mulle.
Means 'I'. Spoken Finnish often says 'mä'.
Ei with -n for 'I': en, I do not.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Means 'is...?'. The question ending -ko turns 'on' (is) into a question.
Sinä with -lla. With on it means 'you have'. Speech shortens it to sul.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Here: in the inessive, literally 'in this'; said when handing something over. Spoken as täs.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.
Speech shortens tämä to tää. Books write tämä.
Speech says vaan. Books write vain.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
After a number the noun takes the partitive: kymmenen minuuttia. Speech turns -ia into -ii.
Voida, can, with -n for 'I': voin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Sinä with -lle for 'to, for'. Speech shortens it to sulle.
Adds -ksi: vastine becomes vastineeksi, 'in return'. Speech drops the last i.
Books write sovittu, 'agreed'. Speech often says diili, from English 'deal'.
